To transform raw text into a numeric representation, simply pass the text to the embed_large method of the loaded model. The raw text should be an object of the class LargeDataSetForText. To create such a data set, please refer to Section 2.

The resulting object can then be passed to the predict method of our classifier to obtain predictions together with an estimate of certainty for each class/category.

# If your classifier is not loaded
classifier <- load_from_disk("examples/cls_imdb_movie_reviews")

# predict the classes of new texts
predicted_categories <- classifier$predict(
  newdata = review_embeddings,
  batch_size = 32
)

# Show predicted categories
head(predicted_categories)
#>             neg        pos expected_category
#> 11329 0.4203428 0.57965720               pos
#> 10460 0.8388274 0.16117263               neg
#> 10536 0.9406573 0.05934272               neg
#> 12035 0.9056520 0.09434797               neg
#> 7267  0.4405586 0.55944151               pos
#> 4761  0.8755952 0.12440486               neg

# Count frequencies
table(predicted_categories$expected_category)
#> 
#> neg pos 
#>  90 210

Once the prediction has been made by the classifier, the estimated categories/classes are stored as ‘predicted_categories’. This object is a data.frame containing text IDs in the rows and the probabilities of the different categories/classes in the columns. The final column, named ‘expected_category’, represents the category assigned to a text with the highest probability.

These estimates can be used in further analyses employing common methods from the educational and social sciences, such as correlation analysis, regression analysis, structural equation modelling, latent class analysis, and analysis of variance.

Now you are ready to to use aifeducation.

7 Feature Extractors

7.1 Introduction

Another way to improve a model’s performance and/or computational speed is to apply a feature extractor. For example, the work of Ganesan et al. (2021) suggests that reducing the hidden size can improve a model’s accuracy. In aifeducation, a feature extractor is a model that reduces the number of features of given text embeddings before feeding the embeddings as input to a classifier.

The feature extractors implemented in aifeducation are auto-encoders that support sequential data and sequences of different lengths. The basic architecture of all the extractors is shown in the following figure.

Figure 18: Basic architecture of feature extractors

The learning objective of the feature extractors is to compress information by reducing the number of features to that of the latent space (Frochte 2019, p. 281). In the figure above, this would mean reducing the number of features from eight to four and storing as much information as possible from eight dimensions in four dimensions. Next, the extractor attempts to reconstruct the original information from the compressed latent space information (Frochte 2019, pp. 280–281). The information is then extended from four dimensions to eight. After training, the hidden representation of the latent space is used as a pre-processing of the original input.

7.2 Creation

In this example, we use the text embeddings from Section 4. You can create a feature extractor as follows:

feature_extractor <- TEFeatureExtractor$new()
feature_extractor$configure(
  label = "Feature extractor for Text Embeddings",
  text_embeddings = review_embeddings,
  features = 384,
  te_n_layers=4,
  method = "Dense",
  orthogonal_method = "matrix_exp",
  noise_factor = 1e-4
)

As with the other models, you can use the label for the model’s label. The argument text_embeddings takes an object of class EmbeddedText or LargeDataSetForTextEmbeddings. This object connects your feature extractor to a specific TextEmbeddingModel. In other words, the feature extractor only works with embeddings from the same TextEmbeddingModel.

The value of the features argument determines the number of features for the compressed representation. The lower the number, the higher the requested compression. This value corresponds to the features of the latent space in the above figure. The te_n_layers parameter allows you you to specify the number of layers in the encoder and decoder parts of the model.

Use this value depending on the number of features of the underlying text embedding model. You can request this value by calling the method get_n_features as follows:

tem$get_n_features()
#> [1] 768

A study by Takeshita et al. (2025) shows that randomly dropping 50% of the dimensions leads only to a minor decrease in the performance of classification tasks. Therefore, this value can be used as a rule of thumb when determining this parameter. We therefore reduce the number of features to 50% to 384.

The type of layer that the feature extractor should use is determined by method. If you set the method to “LSTM”, all layers of the model are long short-term memory layers. If you set the method to “Dense”, all layers are standard dense layers.

Regardless of your choice, all models aim to generate a latent space in which the correlation of the features is zero. Thus, all features represent unique information. In addition, all methods except “LSTM” use an orthogonal parameterisation to prevent overfitting and apply parameter sharing. The opposite layers use the same parameters. For more details, please refer to Ranjan (2019).

You can use the noise_factor to add noise during training, causing the feature extractor to perform as a denoising auto-encoder. This can provide more robust generalisations. Since we work with high batch sizes, we set this value to 1e-4.

7.3 Training

Training the extractor is identical to that for the other models. aifeducation. Please note that the text embeddings provided to data_embeddings must be generated using the same TextEmbeddingModel as the embeddings provided when configuring your model.

feature_extractor$train(
  data_embeddings = review_embeddings,
  data_val_size = 0.25,
  sustain_track = TRUE,
  sustain_iso_code = "DEU",
  sustain_region = NULL,
  sustain_interval = 15,
  sustain_log_level = "error",
  epochs = 8000,
  batch_size = 128,
  lr_rate = 0.0,
  lr_min = 0.0,
  lr_epochs = 30,
  lr_scheduler = "Linear",
  trace = TRUE,
  ml_trace = 1,
  optimizer = "AdamW",
  amp = TRUE,
  lr_warm_up_ratio = 0.10,
  comp_use=TRUE,
  comp_mode="reduce-overhead"
)
#> 2026-09-19 06:22:41 Start
#> Batch size is to big. Change batch size from 128 to 74.
#> 2026-09-19 06:22:41 Start Sustainability Tracking
#> 2026-09-19 06:22:41 Estimating Learning Rates

In this example, we use the same text embeddings that we use to train the classifier. It can be beneficial to use a larger sample of texts when training a TEFeatureExtractor to improve performance and/or allow broader application of the feature extractor.

feature_extractor$plot_learning_rate()

Figure 18: Analysis of Different Learning Rates

You can plot the model’s training history using:

feature_extractor$plot_training_history(
  ind_best_model = TRUE
)

Figure 19: Training History of a Feature Extractor.

Calling print gives you a short summary of the extractor.

print(feature_extractor)
#> Object      : TEFeatureExtractor
#> ID          : tefe_7EFzgxaW56XIsWvY
#> Label       : Feature extractor for Text Embeddings
#> Configured  : TRUE
#> Trained     : TRUE
#> Times       : 3
#> Features In : 768
#> Features Out: 384
#> Parameter   : 1363968

Let us investigate how the feature extractor decreased the correlation between the features. First we calculate the correlations of the uncompressed embeddings.

embeddings_converted=review_embeddings$convert_to_EmbeddedText()
correlations=embeddings_converted$calc_feature_correlation()

correlations$effect_sizes$mean
#>      Mean 
#> 0.5152205
correlations$effect_sizes$sd
#> [1] 0.2524989

Now we calculate the compressed embeddings and estimate the correlation

embeddings_compressed=feature_extractor$extract_features_large(
  review_embeddings,
  batch_size = 32L
  )

embeddings_compressed_converted=embeddings_compressed$convert_to_EmbeddedText()
correlations_compressed=embeddings_compressed_converted$calc_feature_correlation()

correlations_compressed$effect_sizes$mean
#>       Mean 
#> 0.09465684
correlations_compressed$effect_sizes$sd
#> [1] 0.1115881

As you can see the correlation significantly decreased. That is, the feature dimension contain less overlapping information which may lead to a faster and/or better performance of a classifier. Lets try how training change in the following section.

7.4 Application

Once you have trained your feature extractor, you can use it with any classifier. Simply pass the feature extractor to the feature_extractor parameter during the classifier configuration process. Please note that you now have to set the values for feat_size and cls_pooling_features depending on the number of features of the feature extractor, and not depending on the number of features of the text embedding model, since the aim of the feature extractor is to reduce this number. feat_size should be equal to or less than the number of features of the feature extractor, and cls_pooling_features should be equal to or less than feat_size. For the classifier described in Section 6, this would look like this:

classifier_with_fe <- TEClassifierSequential$new()
classifier_with_fe$configure(
  label = "Classifier for Estimating a Postive or Negative Rating of Movie Reviews",
  text_embeddings = review_embeddings,
  feature_extractor = feature_extractor,
  target_levels = c("neg", "pos"),
  skip_connection_type = "ResidualGate",
  cls_pooling_features = 20,
  cls_pooling_type = "WeightedAverageTimes",
  cls_head_type = "Regular",
  cls_input_normalize="PowerNorm",
  final_normalization_type="RMSNorm",
  feat_act_fct = "None",
  feat_size = 128,
  feat_bias = FALSE,
  feat_dropout = 0.05,
  feat_parametrizations = "None",
  feat_normalization_type = "RMSNorm",
  ng_conv_act_fct = "GELU",
  ng_conv_n_layers = 0,
  ng_conv_ks_min = 1,
  ng_conv_ks_max = 2,
  ng_conv_bias = FALSE,
  ng_conv_dropout = 0.40,
  ng_conv_parametrizations = "None",
  ng_conv_normalization_type = "RMSNorm",
  ng_conv_residual_type = "ResidualGate",
  dense_act_fct = "GELU",
  dense_n_layers = 3,
  dense_dropout = 0.40,
  dense_bias = FALSE,
  dense_parametrizations = "None",
  dense_normalization_type = "RMSNorm",
  dense_residual_type = "ResidualGate",
  rec_act_fct = "Tanh",
  rec_n_layers = 0,
  rec_type = "GRU",
  rec_bidirectional = FALSE,
  rec_dropout = 0.2,
  rec_bias = FALSE,
  rec_parametrizations = "None",
  rec_normalization_type = "RMSNorm",
  rec_residual_type = "ResidualGate",
  tf_act_fct = "SwiGLU",
  tf_dense_dim = ceiling(2.67 * 384),
  tf_n_layers = 0,
  tf_dropout_rate_1 = 0.1,
  tf_dropout_rate_2 = 0.3,
  tf_attention_type = "MultiHead",
  tf_positional_type = "absolute",
  tf_num_heads = 4,
  tf_bias = FALSE,
  tf_parametrizations = "None",
  tf_normalization_type = "RMSNorm",
  tf_normalization_position = "Post",
  tf_residual_type = "ResidualGate"
)

That’s all. You can now use and train the classifier in the same way as before, without a feature extractor. You don’t even need to save and load the feature extractor manually. This is done automatically for all classifiers.

classifier_with_fe$train(
  data_embeddings = review_embeddings,
  data_targets = review_labels,
  data_folds = 10,
  data_val_size = 0.25,
  loss_balance_class_weights = TRUE,
  loss_balance_sequence_length = TRUE,
  loss_cls_fct_name = "FocalLoss",
  use_sc = TRUE,
  sc_method = "knnor",
  sc_min_k = 1,
  sc_max_k = 10,
  use_pl = FALSE,
  pl_max_steps = 3,
  pl_max = 1.00,
  pl_anchor = 1.00,
  pl_min = 0.00,
  sustain_track = TRUE,
  sustain_iso_code = "DEU",
  sustain_region = NULL,
  sustain_interval = 15,
  sustain_log_level = "error",
  epochs = 2000,
  batch_size = 128,
  trace = TRUE,
  ml_trace = 1,
  log_dir = NULL,
  log_write_interval = 10,
  n_cores = auto_n_cores(),
  lr_rate = 0.0,
  lr_min = 0.0,
  lr_epochs = 30,
  lr_scheduler = "Linear",
  lr_warm_up_ratio = 0.10,
  optimizer = "AdamW",
  amp = TRUE,
  comp_use=TRUE,
  comp_mode="reduce-overhead"
)

  ind_selected_model = TRUE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10
)

7.5. Saving and Loading

If you would like to save and load a TEFeatureExtractor independently of a classifier, you can use the save_to_disk and load_from_disk functions, as with the other objects of this package. This is useful if you want to use the TEFeatureExtractor at a later point in time in combination with other models.

save_to_disk(
  object = feature_extractor,
  dir_path = "examples",
  folder_name = "feature_extractor"
)

8 Plots for Training History

8.1 BaseModels

You can use BaseModels, TEFeatureExtractors and classifiers to create plots showing your model’s training process. The process of requesting these plots is similar for all objects. However, classifiers offer the greatest degree of customisation of graphics. This chapter demonstrates how to use the plots. We refer to models from previous chapters to provide examples.

We start with the base models. The x_min, x_max, y_min and y_max arguments allow you to zoom in or out. If you set these arguments to NULL, the values will be determined automatically.

The ind_best_model argument allows you to emphasise the epoch with the lowest loss for the validation sample. In general, this is the state of the model with the best generalisation abilities. Unlike the classifiers, this is also the final state of the model after training. The text_size argument allows you to increase or decrease the size of the text within the graphic.

base_model_bert$plot_training_history(
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  ind_best_model = TRUE,
  text_size = 10L
)

Figure 26: Example of a Training History for a BaseModel emphasizing the Best Model State.

8.2 Classifiers

Classifiers offer a greater variety of options. Using the x_min, x_max, y_min and y_max arguments, you can specify the area to be plotted. Setting these arguments to NULL will generate adequate values automatically. With the measure argument, you can select the metric you would like to see. For example, the following plot shows loss.

classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "loss",
  ind_best_model = FALSE,
  ind_selected_model = FALSE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10L
)

Figure 27: Example of a Training History for a Classifier emphasizing the Loss.

The following plot shows how the average iota values changed over the course of the training process.

classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "avg_iota",
  ind_best_model = FALSE,
  ind_selected_model = FALSE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10L
)

Figure 28: Example of a Training History for a Classifier emphasizing the Average Iota.

Setting ind_best_model to TRUE will display additional points in the graphic. These points represents the epochs and their corresponding values according to the chosen metric at which the model performed best. For metrics such as loss, the values should be close to 0, while for metrics such as accuracy, balanced accuracy and average iota, the best values are close to 1. You can see one point for every fold during training.

classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "loss",
  ind_best_model = TRUE,
  ind_selected_model = FALSE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10L
)

Figure 29: Example of a Training History for a Classifier emphasizing the Loss and the best Model States. 

classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "avg_iota",
  ind_best_model = TRUE,
  ind_selected_model = FALSE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10L
)

Figure 30: Example of a Training History for a Classifier emphasizing the Average Iota and the best Model States.

Please note that these points indicate the model’s optimal state according to the chosen metric for each fold. However, these values do not necessarily reflect the final state of the model. This is because the best state of a model during each training loop is determined by the best smoothed average iota value. If there are multiple models with the same smoothed average iota value, the model with the best loss is taken into account. Finally, the state with the highest number of epochs is used.

Set ind_selected_model to TRUE to add the final states of the model for every fold.

classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "loss",
  ind_best_model = TRUE,
  ind_selected_model = TRUE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10L
)

Figure 31: Example of a Training History for a Classifier emphasizing the Loss, the best Model States, and the Final Model States.

Since the performance of a model is determined by several factors, the minimum and maximum values provide a deeper understanding of the training process. To include these in the plot, set add_min_max to TRUE. The plot will now show the full range of values for each epoch according to the chosen metric.

classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "loss",
  ind_best_model = TRUE,
  ind_selected_model = TRUE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = TRUE,
  text_size = 10L
)

Figure 32: Example of a Training History for a Classifier emphasizing the Loss with Minimal and Maximal Values.

Using the argument final_training, you can switch between the performance estimation stage and the final training stage of the model. Since the final training phase only differentiates between training and validation data sets, there is no line for test data. In addition, there are no folds. Therefore, the argument add_min_max has no functionality.

classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = TRUE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "loss",
  ind_best_model = TRUE,
  ind_selected_model = TRUE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = TRUE,
  text_size = 10L
)

Figure 33: Example of a Training History for a Classifier emphasizing the Loss at the Final Training Phase.

The final important argument is pl_step. This value is only relevant if the model used pseudo labeling during training. This parameter allows you to select the step during pseudo labeling that should be displayed in the plot. This works for performance estimation as well as the final training stage.
